title: Le --- To Him, To Her, To You

lessons.title: le — "to him," "to her," "to you"
lessons.gloss: "to him, to her, to you" — a Latin case Spanish kept and English threw away

segments.text: Lo and la answer the question what. This chapter answers a different one: to whom.
le — to him, to her, to you (with usted).
Le digo. — I tell him. Or her. Or you.

Some verbs land on a thing: you have it, you make it, you want it. Others land on a person you are aiming at — you tell them, you speak to them, you give them something. Spanish uses a different pronoun for the second kind, and le is it.
Same slot. Still in front of the verb. Nothing about the shape of a sentence has changed in eleven chapters.
And here is the relief: le does not mark gender.
Le digo. — I tell him. and I tell her. and I tell you.

After four chapters of choosing between lo and la by the gender of a noun, this one asks you for nothing. One form covers three people. If you need to say which, you add it in words — but the pronoun itself does not care.
Lo and le are the same Latin word again — and this time the difference is not wear, it is grammar.
Latin changed a word's ending to show its job in the sentence. Ille, "that one," had one form for the thing an action hit and another for the person it was aimed at:
illum — the one the verb acts on becomes Spanish lo.
illī — the one it is aimed at becomes Spanish le.

Latin called these the accusative and the dative. Almost all of that system collapsed on the way to Spanish; nouns lost their endings entirely. But in these small, constantly-used pronouns, two of the cases survived, and you are looking at them.

English had the same distinction and lost it more completely. It survives in a word order rather than a shape: I told him the story — him is doing exactly what le does, and English simply stopped marking it.

feedback.correct: And the same two words mean I tell her.

segments.prompt: How many genders does le have?

feedback.correct: One form for him, her and usted.
feedback.incorrect: None — unlike lo and la, le does not mark gender at all.

segments.prompt: Lo comes from Latin illum. Which Latin form does le come from, and what was it for?
acceptedResponses: illi, for the one the action is aimed at

feedback.correct: Two Latin cases, both still alive in these two small words.
feedback.incorrect: Illi — the dative, the form for whoever the verb was aimed at.

segments.text: Say "I tell him." (Le digo.) And "I tell her." (Le digo — the same.) Which Latin case is le? (The dative, illī.) Next: its plural, and a discovery about how little of this system is actually new.
